activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: In his 'Rhetoric', Aristotle described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, reasoning and evidence.
story:
Addisson had signed up for drama camp expecting improv games, not debate, but on the first Tuesday Ms. Sharma announced a mock trial about whether the camp's ancient furnace should be replaced. "Building a case is acting too," she said. "You're performing an argument." Addison wanted the lead role, which meant she had to build a case with a claim, evidence, and a warrant for every point, and she had no idea what a warrant was.

Her team drew the side against replacement, which felt impossible. Everyone in the rehearsal hall had frozen in the same draft all week. Jaiveer wanted to open with a story about a little kid shivering in the hallway. "It'll make the judges cry," he said. "Crying wins."

Their opponents, led by Andrei, showed up with a clipboard. He rattled off numbers: repair logs, temperature readings, the cost of a new boiler against ten more years of patching. He didn't raise his voice once. When Jaiveer told his shivering story, one judge nodded, but the other two kept writing on their pads, and when the verdict came, the numbers team won. Addison stared at the score sheet and felt something shift in her head, like finding the mechanism inside a magic trick. The sad story had moved people, but it hadn't proved anything.

That night she couldn't hibernate like the camp rabbit in the nature hut display; she lay awake turning it over. In the camp library she found a battered copy of Aristotle's "Rhetoric" and read until her flashlight dimmed. The next morning she found Jaiveer at breakfast. "He said there are three ways to persuade," she told him. "Ethos, pathos, and logos. Pathos is the emotions, like your story. Logos is reasoning and evidence, like Andrei's clipboard. And ethos is whether the judges trust the speaker." Jaiveer set down his toast. "So we used one out of three."

"Exactly. We need all three." They spent a tedious afternoon rebuilding the case. Claim: the furnace should not be replaced this year. Evidence: the repair records and the budget numbers, checked twice. Warrant: if the records show the furnace has broken down only once in three years, and the camp needs that money for scholarships, then replacement can wait. Addison practiced her delivery until the other campers started calling her "the lawyer."

At the rematch, Andrei raised an eyebrow at her new clipboard but stuck to his old speech, smooth and confident. Addison gave the numbers first, then, at the end, one story, about a camper who might not come back next year without the scholarship fund. She watched the second judge put down her pen. When Ms. Sharma called the debate for Addison's team, Jaiveer grabbed her arm and lifted it like a referee. "The lawyer rests," he said, and the whole hall laughed.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: Nicotine's effects fade quickly because the body clears about half of it in roughly two hours, so users soon feel the urge for another dose.
story:
Anna slid her presentation notes across the lab table so Alanna could see them. "The reward pathway," she said, tapping her diagram of the brain. "That's the part nicotine hijacks. It floods the pathway with dopamine, and the brain learns to want it again."

Mr. Malik had given them a week to prepare their health talk, and Anna had spent most of it drawing arrows on her poster. The arrows were the easy part. The hard part was the question he kept asking: not just what nicotine did, but why people couldn't simply stop.

"It's like being hungry," Alanna offered. "Sort of."

"Except you can postpone lunch," Anna said. "My cousin Marcus vapes, and he can't postpone anything. Last summer he got restless at my house every couple of hours and had to go outside. Every time. I used to think he just liked standing in the driveway."

She thought about that summer now, how she'd teased him about it, and how his jaw had tightened before he laughed. She hadn't understood what she was watching. Maybe she should have.

"Wait," Alanna said slowly. "Every couple of hours. Like clockwork?"

Anna pulled out her phone and found the note she'd made in August, back when she'd started counting out of curiosity. 10:15, driveway. 12:30, driveway. 2:40, driveway. "I looked it up this morning," she said. "The body clears about half the nicotine in roughly two hours. That's why the effect fades so fast and he'd get the urge for another dose. His brain wanted the pathway flooded again, and the level in his blood kept dropping."

"So his brain isn't broken," Alanna said. "It's just following a schedule he never asked for."

"Basically." Anna taped her diagram to the whiteboard, then stood back and frowned at it. The arrows went one direction only. She uncapped a marker and drew a loop: nicotine in, dopamine up, level falls, urge, nicotine in again. "We should present it like this. Not a straight line. A circle."

During fifth period, Payton wandered over to their table while they practiced. "You're going to tell everyone my brother's got a two-hour timer in his head?" she said. She didn't sound angry, exactly, but she didn't smile either.

"I'm not naming anyone," Anna said. "Just the science." She hesitated, because last summer she'd named Marcus to half the neighborhood as a joke. "I didn't get it back then. I do now."

Payton picked up the marker and added a small stick figure on the loop, right where the urge was. "Put him there," she said. "That's exactly what Ty looks like when he's waiting."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: In Hinduism, moksha is liberation from the cycle of rebirth, and it is considered the highest goal of human life.
story:
The bell above the door of his grandfather's study had a way of announcing Oliver before he could knock, and today it rang twice because his elbow caught it on the way in. He was carrying a notebook with a school assignment folded inside: compare how two faiths explain what happens after death. He had until Monday, and so far his page had one word on it, which was "heaven," and a doodle of a cloud.

"Grandpa, can I ask you something for my project?" He set the notebook on the desk between a jar of pens and a small brass lamp that his grandfather lit every morning. "You're Hindu, and Grandma was raised going to church. So you two believed really different things, right?"

His grandfather put down his newspaper. "Sit. Ask."

Oliver sat on the stiff wooden chair he had sat on since he was six, when his feet had not reached the floor. "Okay. So in church they say you go to heaven, and that's the best thing. And in Hinduism you get reborn. So is being reborn the good part? Like, the reward?"

His grandfather's eyebrows went up, and Oliver knew he had gotten something wrong, the same feeling as handing in a math test and watching the teacher pause at question four.

"Let me show you something." His grandfather opened a drawer and took out a photograph, luminous in the lamplight, of Oliver's great-grandmother standing in a doorway with her hands folded. "She was a veteran of many things, your great-grandmother. Hard years, good years. Suppose she is born again after this life. Then born again after that. And again. A wheel that keeps turning."

"Forever?"

"For a very long time. Now, is that what she would hope for, or escape from?"

Oliver looked at the photograph. The woman in it looked tired in a patient way, like someone who had carried a lot and set it down carefully. He turned his pencil over in his fingers, thinking. If heaven was the goal in Grandma's old church, then maybe Hinduism had a goal too, and maybe the goal was not more turns of the wheel. "So there's something past the wheel," he said slowly. "Getting off it."

His grandfather smiled, one of his small ones that Oliver had to earn. "It is called moksha," he said. "Liberation from the cycle of rebirth. It is the highest goal of human life."

Oliver wrote it down, spelling it twice under his breath to get it right. Then he read back what he had. "So both of them have a highest thing. Heaven for Grandma's church, moksha for yours. They're not the same, but they're both like, the top of the mountain." He paused. "Different paths up it?"

"That is your project, beta. I only answer questions."

Oliver grinned and flipped to a fresh page to make a chart. He would allocate one column to each faith, with rebirth and the stopping of rebirth on one side and heaven on the other, and he would need more room than Monday allowed. Footsteps came down the hall, and his grandmother appeared with a plate of sliced mango, setting it between the notebook and the lamp without a word, the way she always did when she knew he would be there awhile.

"Take two pieces," his grandfather said, pushing the plate toward him. "You have a mountain to draw."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Evelyn jammed her backpack into the seat beside her and pulled out the folded printout of the district swim standings. The bus rattled out of the school lot, and she smoothed the paper on her knee. There it was: Ridgeview relays, ranked first; her own team, ranked second. One spot. Two weeks until the final meet.

"You're staring again," said Louka, dropping into the seat across the aisle. She held up her phone, screen out. "Kylian's mom recorded the state finals from TV. Watch this race, the hundred-meter freestyle. It's insane."

Evelyn leaned over. Two swimmers hit the wall nearly together, and the clock on the screen split them: one finished in 47.31, the other in 47.32.

"A hundredth of a second," Louka breathed. "That's a blink. That's less than a blink." She replayed it three times, and Evelyn watched the silver medalist's face each time, like she was hoping the ending might change.

Evelyn sat back. Second place by a hundredth of a second. Her team was second in the district standings. She had been picturing her team as just barely behind Ridgeview, close enough to touch, because that was what second place felt like. But the rankings never said how far apart first and second actually were. The gap could be a hundredth of a second, or it could be a whole minute. She dug into her bag for a pencil. On the back of the printout she copied the times listed under the standings: Ridgeview's season-best relay, then her team's. She subtracted. Seven seconds. Seven whole seconds, not seven hundredths. She let that digest while the bus swayed around the corner by the bakery.

"That's not a blink," she said out loud.

"What?" Louka looked up.

"The rankings only show order. They don't show distance. We could be behind by a hundredth or by a minute, and the paper looks exactly the same." She tapped the standings. "I did the math. We're seven seconds back. I thought we were close. We're not close."

Louka's shoulders dropped, but then she lifted the phone again. "Okay, but watch this one. The same silver medalist, a different year." On the screen, the swimmer lost by a margin so wide the camera cut away before she touched the wall. "Second place again," Louka said quietly. "Same rank. Totally different race. I keep watching her because I want to figure out what she does after she loses. She wrote a memoir about it, did I tell you? My mom ordered it. The cover says she came back and won the next season."

Kylian shoved down the aisle and grabbed the pole, out of breath. "Coach posted the lineup. Evelyn, you're anchoring the relay." He grinned. "You. The last leg. Seven seconds is a lot, but the anchor swims against their anchor, and their anchor had a bad taper last year, and if you go out fast and hold, and Louka gains on the second leg, and we all drop half a second, that's two seconds right there, and relays are weird, anything can happen."

"Half a second each," Evelyn said, writing it down, the numbers suddenly durable and real on the page instead of a fog of worry. "Louka, second leg. That's you."

Louka closed the video and sat up straight. "Then I'm not just watching the silver medalist anymore. I'm going to swim like her next year, after she came back."

The bus hissed to a stop at the corner by the pool, and Kylian was already first through the doors, shouting, "Seven seconds! Let's go eat them!"

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: In layers of rock that have not been flipped or disturbed, the lowest layers are the oldest, an idea called the law of superposition.
story:
The trail dropped toward the river just as the sun cleared the ridge, and Elizabeth stopped so suddenly that Annabel bumped into her backpack. Below them the canyon walls rose in bands of color, red and cream and a thin stripe of black near the bottom, like a layer cake cut open by the river itself.

"We have to figure this out before Ms. Navarro's talk tonight," Elizabeth said, pulling out her notebook. Their assignment was to explain, at the campfire, how a river could carve a canyon over millions of years, and she had promised to have an answer that made sense.

Braelynn crouched at the edge and pointed at the highest stripe, a pale band near the rim. "I bet that top layer is the oldest. It's the biggest one, so it must have taken the longest to make."

Elizabeth wrote it down, then frowned at it. Something about the guess bothered her, though she couldn't say what. "Let's test it," she said. "Not the whole canyon. Something small."

Below the trail, a side stream trickled down a slope of sand and gravel left by earlier floods. Elizabeth found a flat tin plate from her cook kit and set it in the streambed where the water slowed. "If the river drops stuff when it slows down, then whatever lands first should end up underneath." Annabel poured a handful of dark gravel into the current upstream, and after some of it tumbled past, a few pebbles sank onto the plate. Then Braelynn poured white sand. It settled over the dark pebbles in a thin, even sheet.

Elizabeth tipped the plate out, studied the little pile, and felt her stomach jump. The white sand sat on top. The dark pebbles, which had arrived first, lay on the bottom. She scribbled a quick sketch. "The stuff that gets dropped first is on the bottom. So the bottom layer is the oldest, not the top."

"That's for our plate," Braelynn said, chin up toward the canyon. "The real thing is different."

"It's not, though." Elizabeth pointed at the black stripe far below them, just above the water. "The river has been dropping and piling up layers since before anything was alive here to watch. Each new layer lands on top of the last one. Unless the rocks got flipped or disturbed somehow, the lowest layers are the oldest. I remember the phrase now, from the book in the tent. It's called the law of superposition."

Ms. Navarro came up the trail behind them with a daypack and a thermos, and Elizabeth, guessing she'd say something about not doing all the work for the girls, waited until the teacher had poured her coffee before holding up the plate. "Ms. Navarro, if nobody moved the rock layers around, is the bottom one the oldest?"

Ms. Navarro smiled into her cup. "Go check your pile of sand and pebbles again. What did you just watch happen?"

They spent the rest of the morning at the overlook. Annabel held a penlight at an angle so its beam split through Braelynn's water bottle and threw a wobbly prism of color onto the cream stripe, showing how one layer could look different in changing light, which meant some of their earlier guesses about matching layers were trivial compared with the real question of order. Elizabeth drew the whole wall, bottom to top, labeling the black stripe as the oldest, then tracing with her finger how the river, grinding and carrying and dropping, had cut down through everything they could see.

That evening at the fire, she stood up with her notebook and the tin plate. She told the group about the pebbles and the sand, about the layers piling from the bottom up, about water that never hurried but never stopped, and how a thing too slow to see could still disclose the whole history of a place if you knew how to read it from the bottom up. When she finished, she held the plate above the firelight and let the dark pebbles slide down over the white sand, and everyone leaned in to watch them land.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Bones grow longer at growth plates near their ends, and once these plates close after puberty, a person stops getting taller.
story:
The pencil mark on Annabel's kitchen doorframe read "Annabel, age 12" and it was a full inch above the mark from six months earlier. Kaylee stood beside it while Annabel's mom penciled in a new line, and when it was Kaylee's turn, the line landed exactly where her last one had been. Not even a tiny bit higher.

"Maybe you're just between growth spurts," Annabel said, spinning the pencil between her fingers. "I skipped almost a whole year when I was ten."

Kaylee traced the flat line with her fingertip. "Or maybe I'm finished. My cousin stopped growing in seventh grade and she's still the shortest one in her family." The idea landed in her stomach like a dropped rock. Everything about her had been changing lately, her shoes, her jacket sleeves, even her voice had gone squeaky once during a book report. She had assumed growing came with the rest of it, but what if it didn't?

They carried bowls of popcorn to Annabel's room, where Cruz was already sprawled on the rug assembling a model skeleton he'd gotten for his birthday. "Perfect timing," Annabel said. "Cruz broke his arm last spring. Show her."

Cruz retrieved his phone from under a pillow and pulled up a photo of an X-ray. "That's my radius," he said, pointing to a bone in his forearm. Near the wrist, the bone looked slightly uneven, like two pieces of a puzzle not quite pushed together. "The doctor called that part my growth plate. She said bones grow longer at the growth plates near their ends. That's the whole reason bones get longer at all."

"What happens if it breaks there?" Kaylee asked, leaning closer.

"That's the bad part. She said once the plates close after puberty, that's it. The bone stops getting taller and it's permanent. That's why they watched my arm so carefully." Cruz snapped a tiny bone into place on the model. "Anyway, mine were still wide open, so I got a whole speech about how much taller I'm going to get. Annoying, but kind of good news."

Kaylee sat very still while the pieces fit together in her head. The changes she'd noticed, the squeaky voice, the new curves, the spots on her chin, were all signs of puberty. And puberty was the thing that closed the plates. But closing took time, and the doctor had needed an X-ray to see Cruz's. Nobody could look at a kitchen doorframe and know. So she couldn't actually be sure she was finished, which meant she also couldn't be sure she wasn't.

"Okay," she said. "Experiment. Mark me on your doorframe, and I'll come back every month, and we'll see if the line moves. If it moves even a little, the plates are still open. If it doesn't move for a whole year, I'll ask my mom to book a doctor's appointment and find out for real."

"Scientific," Annabel said, already heading back down the stairs for the pencil. Cruz raised his soda in salute.

At the doorframe, Annabel pressed the pencil gently against the top of Kaylee's head and drew the line, then labeled it with the date. Kaylee studied it, memorizing its exact height against the wood grain, one centimeter below the knot in the wood. "Next month, same door, same pencil," she said. "And if I show up taller, the first thing I'm doing is gloating."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Professional fact-checkers use lateral reading: instead of judging a website by its own pages, they open new tabs to see what other sources say about it.
story:
Cole wanted to win the school's health fair, and he thought he had found the perfect topic. A website called BrightWave Science claimed that their ocean mineral drink could improve memory in just two weeks. The page looked amazing, with photographs of smiling scientists and a chart that climbed upward like a rocket. He printed three pages and carried them to the library table where Kyla and Francois were gluing their poster board.

"You have to see this," Cole said, spreading the pages out. "I'm going to present it Monday."

Francois leaned in and frowned. "Ms. Sun says we need two sources for every claim. Do you have another one?"

Kyla picked up a page before Cole could answer. "Every article on this site mentions BrightWave. Even the one about sleep." She turned the page sideways, as if the problem might be visible from an angle. He felt an acute flash of doubt, sharp and sudden, like stepping off a curb he hadn't seen.

Cole took the pages back. "It says science right in the name." But that night, at his kitchen table, he kept thinking about how the whole site only talked about one drink. He opened his laptop and, instead of reading more of the website's own pages, he opened new tabs and searched for what other sources said about BrightWave. The first tab showed a news story about the company being fined for false advertising. The second showed that the "independent research institute" on the site shared an address with the company itself. The third was a seller's page, because BrightWave didn't just review the drink, it sold it.

At school the next morning he found Kyla at her locker. "You were right. The whole website is theirs." He showed her his notes, which he had spent an hour trying to coordinate into a clear order, sources matched to claims. "I read sideways, kind of. New tabs instead of their own pages."

Kyla smiled. "My cousin calls that lateral reading. She does it for her job."

"My presentation was going to be about a miracle drink," Cole said. The embarrassment burned in his ears, and he stared at the floor of the hallway. "I told Francois it was a sure win."

"So make the presentation about checking instead," Kyla said. "Show the class the pretty website, then show them the tabs."

Cole looked up. He still had the printed pages in his backpack, the smiling scientists and the rocket chart. He pulled them out, folded them in half, and tucked them under his arm. "First tab," he said, and headed for room 214.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim that cannot be checked even in principle, such as a vague promise that something 'changes lives,' gives readers nothing to test.
story:
The flyer had appeared in every locker that morning, and by the time Carter climbed onto the bus, half the kids were already holding one. It showed a boy mid-jump, grinning, with a silver band on his wrist. The words above him said, "LifeBand changes lives."

"Nine dollars," Rachel said, turning her flyer toward the window. "I've saved eleven. I could get one Friday."

Carter squinted at the paper. "Changes lives how? Does it do anything?"

"It changes lives," Rachel repeated, like that settled it. "It says so."

Thatcher leaned over the seat behind them. "My cousin bought one. He wore it for a month and said he felt amazing."

Carter read the flyer again, back to front. There was no number, no measurement, nothing about what the band did or how you'd know. He thought about Mr. Chatterjee's science class, where a claim meant something you could check. "The problem," he said slowly, "is there's no way to test this. It's a claim that can't be checked even in principle. A vague promise that something changes lives gives you nothing to test."

Rachel frowned. "So?"

"So how would you ever know it didn't work? If your life doesn't change, they can just say it would've been worse without it. You can't prove them wrong. It's not like a real claim, like 'this holds ten kilograms' or 'this runs for six hours.'"

Rachel's shoulders dropped a little. "It's still a nice bracelet."

"It is," Carter agreed. "But they're charging nine dollars like it's credible, like there's actual logic behind it, and there isn't any way to check."

The bus rattled over the tracks by the gas station. Thatcher drummed his fingers on the seat. "Okay," he said, "then test it backwards. Rachel wears a plain rubber band for a week and tells everybody it's a LifeBand. If people start saying their lives changed, we'll know it's all in what they were told, not the band."

Rachel sat up. "That's actually a plan."

"Saturday to Saturday," Thatcher said. "Write down anything that happens."

"If my week gets worse," Rachel said, sliding the flyer into her backpack, "does that mean my life would have deteriorated faster without a fake LifeBand? Because that sounds exactly like something a company would say."

Carter laughed. "That's the trap. But we'll have your notes, and we'll have the plan. That's more than that flyer ever gave us."

The bus lurched to a stop at the corner of Maple Street. Rachel pulled the plain rubber band off her stack of homework, snapped it onto her wrist, and held her hand out the aisle toward Carter. "Saturday," she said. "Count me in."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a trumpet valve sends air through an extra loop of tubing, making the air column longer and the note lower.
story:
Isla had wanted to quit the band twice already, once in September and once after the winter concert, when Mr. Malik had asked her to play a solo and she had shaken her head so fast her ponytail whipped her own face. Her grandfather's trumpet sat on his dresser now, in the house where she came every second Saturday, and this time she had actually picked it up. It was heavier than she expected, and the valves felt oily and smooth under her fingers.

"You're finally touching it," her grandfather said from the doorway. "Three years it sat there."

"I'm terrible at it," Isla said. "That's the whole problem." She pressed the first valve down and blew, and a wobbly note came out, flatter and sadder than the open note she'd played a minute before.

He sat down in his chair without saying anything, which was his way of letting her figure something out on her own. She stared at the three valves. In the band room, Karina had asked Mr. Malik how three little buttons could make so many different notes, and he had just smiled and said to listen carefully. Billy had shrugged and gone back to his drumsticks. Isla had thought about it for a week without getting anywhere, and thinking about it was part of why she hadn't quit a third time, because she wanted the answer more than she wanted to be good.

Now she pressed one valve at a time and listened. First valve, lower. Second valve, lower still, but less. Third valve, lower the most. She slid the trumpet off her lap and looked down the tubing, following where the air would go, and saw it: each valve sent the air through an extra loop of tubing, a whole detour it hadn't taken before. More tubing, and the note dropped. That was it. A longer column of air made a lower note, and three valves mixed together could make all those combinations.

"Say something," her grandfather said.

"Pressing a valve makes the air go through an extra loop of tubing," she said. "Longer column, lower note. That's how three valves make so many notes."

He laughed, a dry sound. "Forty years, and you explain it in one breath."

She put the trumpet back to her lips to try the valves in a real combination, took a slow breath, and began to exhale into the mouthpiece, holding the suspense of the note before it broke loose. The sound that came out was cracked and thin, an impoverished little squawk that would have sent her slumping in the band room. She waited for the embarrassment anyway.

Her grandfather was already reaching for the phone on the side table. "Karina's number still on the fridge?" he asked. "She plays horn. She'll want to hear this."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating, because it wears and washes off.
story:
Alexis stood at the end of the dock with a green tube of sunscreen in his fist and a question he couldn't shake. Brennan had slathered the stuff on at breakfast, before anyone even stepped outside, and now Brennan was lying in the infirmary tent with his shoulders striped red. It didn't make sense. Alexis turned the tube over in his hands, reading the tiny letters twice.

"You're going to wear a hole in that label," Lochlan said, dropping onto the dock beside him. His sneakers swung over the water.

"He put it on this morning," Alexis said. "Same stuff, same as mine. So why did he burn and I didn't?"

Lochlan shrugged. "Maybe he's just the burning kind."

Alexis didn't buy it. He thought about the shape of the day, the way you'd map a shoreline from a boat. Brennan had been first in the water at nine and last out at noon, then again after lunch, diving off the dock until Ms. Goldberg called the swim period. Alexis had been in and out too, but he'd climbed up to the dock twice to eat, and both times he'd reapplied, mostly because the tube was in his bag and he was bored. That was the only difference he could find.

"Timing," he said slowly. "It has to be timing."

"Timing of what?"

"Of the sunscreen." He squinted down the lake, where the afternoon counselor was already waving the next group in. "Watch. I'll test it."

The plan was simple, the way the best plans were. Alexis marked the time on his watch, applied the sunscreen, and swam. When two hours passed, or when he got out and toweled off, he reapplied, even when Lochlan groaned about waiting. He felt slightly ridiculous standing on the sun-baked boards, greasy and squinting, while everyone else was already back in the water.

"You look like a glazed doughnut," Lochlan called from the deep.

"Two hours!" Alexis called back, capping the tube.

By evening, when the sun finally let go of the lake and the water went copper, Alexis checked his skin in the washhouse mirror. Nothing. Not even pink. He walked to the infirmary tent to tell Brennan, feeling buoyant, almost bouncing on the packed dirt.

Ms. Goldberg was coming out as he arrived. She caught his arm. "Going to see Brennan?"

"Yes. I figured out why he burned and I didn't." He held up the tube. "You have to put it on again every two hours, and right after swimming or sweating a lot. It washes off. He only did it once, this morning."

She looked at him for a long second, then smiled. "You should tell him exactly that."

Brennan was propped on his cot, miserable and glowing pink. Alexis sat on the edge and held up the green tube.

"Tomorrow," he said, "we go in on a schedule."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: In summer, sunlight strikes the ground more directly, so the same light is concentrated on a smaller area and heats it more.
story:
The flashlight in Theodore's hand trembled as Ms. Tesfaye's science class arranged their chairs in a circle. Tomorrow was the quiz on why Earth has seasons, and he still could not make the answer sit still in his head.

"Volunteers to explain the tilt of Earth's axis," Ms. Tesfaye said. "Theodore, you've been hiding back there. Come up."

He hadn't been concealing himself on purpose, but he had hoped she wouldn't notice him. He stood, and his fingers found the bandage on his wrist where he had pulled a tendon badly enough in soccer practice that the coach made him sit out a week. Even holding a flashlight made the wrist ache a little.

"Okay," he said. "The axis is tilted, so..." He stopped. So what? He knew the words, but the words felt like a costume he was wearing wrong.

"Wait," said Vladimir from the second row. "Before you talk, can you use the flashlight? Trinity said something about it at lunch."

"Flashlight and this," Trinity said, holding up a sheet of white poster board. She smoothed it flat on the desk in front of her. "Go on, point it straight down."

Theodore clicked the light on and aimed it straight down at the board. A small circle glowed on the white surface, bright and hard-edged.

"Now tilt it," Trinity said.

He tipped the flashlight toward one side. The circle stretched into a long oval, and the light went pale, like somebody had stretched the same brightness over too much paper. Vladimir leaned in, still looking skeptical, one eyebrow up.

"It's dimmer," Vladimir said. "Same flashlight. Where did the brightness go?"

"Nowhere," Theodore said slowly. "It's just spread out." He straightened the flashlight again and the small circle snapped back, intense. He tilted it, and the oval widened and faded. Straight, bright. Tilted, dim. Something in his chest lifted, the way a stuck door does when it finally gives.

"Summer," he said. "When our part of Earth is tilted toward the sun, the sunlight comes down more directly, like the flashlight straight up and down. The same light is concentrated on a smaller area, so it heats it more. And in winter, the light comes in at a slant, spread over a bigger area, so it doesn't heat the ground as much." He looked around the circle. Trinity was nodding hard enough to make her braids swing.

"So the seasons aren't about being closer to the sun," Vladimir said. "They're about the angle."

"Right," Theodore said. "The tilt aims the light."

Ms. Tesfaye had not said a word through any of this. Now she held out her hand for the flashlight.

"Quiz question," she said. "Who wants the flashlight next?"

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Near the equator, sunlight stays fairly direct all year, so temperatures change little and many places have wet and dry seasons instead of warm and cold ones.
story:
Ruby dragged the beach ball to the middle of the backyard and jammed a chopstick through it from the recycling bin, which made it look less like Earth and more like a giant lollipop. She had to present on Friday, and her one job was to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons. The problem was that every time she practiced in front of the mirror, she heard herself saying "the tilt" about nine times without once saying anything true.

"You're going to nominate that thing for the science fair?" Reina asked from the porch steps. She had come over with her backpack still on, because she liked to do homework anywhere except her own house.

"It's a model," Ruby said. "Watch. I shine the flashlight, and the tilt means the light hits us at an angle in winter, more spread out. In summer it's more direct." She spun the ball slowly, holding the chopstick at a slant. The flashlight beam made a fat, pale oval on the upper half and a long thin smear on the lower half, which was promising until the chopstick slipped and the ball rolled into the tomato plants.

Reina laughed, but not at the ball. "Four seasons," she said. "That's such a strange thing to have to explain."

"What do you mean?"

"I lived near the equator until I was nine. Nobody there talks about warm and cold seasons. It's wet season and dry season, that's it." Reina picked a tomato leaf and shredded it into tiny pieces. "When I got here and everyone was so excited about autumn, I thought you were all pretending."

Ruby sat down on the step beside her. "But the tilt," she said slowly. The tilt should have made seasons everywhere, and Reina's old home was on the same tilted Earth. She got the flashlight and the ball back and tried again, keeping the chopstick steady this time. When she aimed the light straight down at the middle of the ball, the beam made a tight, bright circle no matter how she spun it. Above and below the middle, the light stretched out thin. That was it. Near the equator, sunlight stayed fairly direct all year, so the temperature barely changed, and people counted wet and dry seasons instead of warm and cold ones. The seasons Reina grew up with weren't wrong; they were just a different part of the same spinning ball.

"You have to be in my presentation," Ruby said. "You say the wet and dry part. Mr. Lin said we could bring a partner."

"I can't. We're moving back in June." Reina said it to the shredded leaf in her hand, not to Ruby. "That's why I've been doing homework at everyone's house but mine. It's too quiet there with all the boxes."

Ruby looked at the ball, its fat bright circle still shining in the dimming yard. "Then do it anyway. One time. Friday." Somewhere under the tomato plants, a pill bug curled into its shell, one more decomposer cleaning up the mess she'd made, doing its small work whether anyone watched or not.

Reina tossed the shredded leaf onto the compost pile and stood. "Fine. But if I mess up the word equator in front of everyone, that's on you."

"Deal," Ruby said, and shone the flashlight on her, straight and bright.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Snapchat's Snap Map, launched in 2017, can show a user's real-time location to their friends on a map.
story:
Ella stared at her phone in the food court of the mall, waiting for Robyn to text back. In their group chat, Vanessa had just written, "Want me to save you a spot in line at the game store? It's getting long." But Ella had never told anyone which store she was heading to.

She typed, "How did you know I'm going there?" Vanessa replied with a screenshot of a map dotted with tiny friend emojis, including one labeled Ella, sitting right on top of the game store across the mall. "It's called Snap Map," Vanessa wrote. "It can show your real-time location to your friends on a map."

Eella felt her stomach drop. Her plan had been to buy a birthday gift for Robyn in secret, and Robyn was in the same group chat, with the same map. The party was tomorrow at noon, which meant she had about an hour before the mall closed. If Robyn opened that map, she would see Ella's dot parked outside the store with the exact game Robyn had been talking about for weeks.

She tested a theory. She walked two stores down and stood outside a shoe shop, then texted Vanessa, "Check the map. Where am I now?" Vanessa answered, "Shoe store. Ooh, are you getting the blue sneakers?" The dot moved when Ella moved, in real time, like a little shadow she could not shake. So Ella tried turning her location sharing off for Robyn only, keeping it on for Vanessa, and asked Vanessa to check again. "Your dot disappeared from Robyn's side," Vanessa confirmed, "but I can still see you. Try the bookstore." Ella walked there, and Vanessa reported the change within seconds.

Her abrupt plan worked, but guilt nibbled at her for hiding something from Robyn, even for a good reason. She bought the game, wrapped it in a bag from the bookstore to insulate the surprise, and hurried to the exit as the overhead speakers announced the mall would close in fifteen minutes.

The next day at the party, Robyn tore open the gift and shrieked. "How did you get this without me seeing? I checked the map last night and your dot was at your house the whole time."

Ella grinned and held up her phone. "Let's just say I learned to disappear."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 2 is the only even prime number, because every larger even number can be divided evenly by 2.
story:
The computer lab was humid from thirty machines running all afternoon, and Hayden's program still refused to cooperate. He had written it himself, line by line in Python, following the plan from the whiteboard: ask for a number, test whether anything divides it, print "prime" or "not prime." It worked for 7. It worked for 15, which correctly came out not prime. Then Caelan leaned over his shoulder and typed 2, and the screen said not prime.

"That's wrong," Hayden said. "Two has to be prime. There's nothing to divide it by except one and itself." He scrolled up through his loop, looking for a mistake. Caelan pointed at the first line of the test, where Hayden had told the program to reject every even number before doing anything else. It seemed sensible when he wrote it. Even numbers felt like the opposite of prime.

Lorelai pulled her chair over from the next station. "Run it with eight," she said. He typed 8, and the program said not prime. Then 9, and it said not prime, because three divides nine. He tried 10, 12, 14. All not prime, all correct. The program was getting the big evens right and the small one wrong, which was a contradiction he couldn't ignore. Something about the number 2 was different from every other even number, and the difference was invisible in his code.

He whispered the sequence to himself, testing each even number in his head like the program would. Four. Six. Eight. Every one of them could be split into equal halves, which meant something divided each of them besides one and themselves. But when he reached 2, the splitting stopped. There was nothing left over to divide it. He sat back. "Two is the only even prime number," he said slowly, "because every larger even number can be divided evenly by 2."

"Then fix the loop," Caelan said.

Haydan deleted the line that threw out all evens and added a special case instead: if the number is 2, print prime. He ran the program again and typed 2. The word prime appeared in green, and he transmitted a screenshot to the club's shared folder so Lorelai could check it from her machine. Ms. Yoon walked past and paused at his screen, but she only nodded and kept moving.

He tried 2 one more time, then 97, watching both answers come back. "Okay," he said to the screen. "Now try to break it."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: In a 2007 study, people kept awake for a whole night showed about 60 percent stronger reactions to upsetting pictures in the amygdala, a brain area that responds to threats.
story:
The night before the canoe regatta, Lacey had talked Olivia and Celina into staying awake until the meteors came. "It's the best shower in ten years," she had whispered, spreading her sleeping bag on the dock. "Sleeping is optional. Stars are mandatory." They had watched until three, seen exactly four streaks, and then Olivia had gotten maybe two hours of restless dozing before the whistle blew.

The morning went wrong in small ways. Olivia dropped her paddle twice, and when Celina joked about it, "Nice catch, Olivia, oh wait," Olivia's throat went hot and her eyes stung, and she snapped, "Shut up, Celina," loud enough that two counselors turned around. Celina's face went pale. Olivia sat in the stern, stunned at herself. It was a tiny joke. Celina made jokes like that every single day.

That evening, while the others were at the campfire, Olivia found Celina scrubbing the paddles at the wash stand. "I'm sorry about today," Olivia said. Celina kept scrubbing. "You never yell at me." "I know. I've been trying to figure out why I did." She told Celina her theory: it wasn't the joke, and it wasn't her. It was the missing night of sleep, though she couldn't see that anywhere in her body, the way you can't see wind, only what it knocks over. Mr. Szabó, the nature instructor, had mentioned something at dinner about tired brains, and she wanted to check it.

They found him coiling rope by the boathouse. "Celina," Olivia said, "tell him what you looked up on your phone in the infirmary." Celina still wanted her apology acknowledged, Olivia could tell, so she added, "Please. Then I'll do the rest." Celina recited it flat, like a price: "In a 2007 study, people kept awake for a whole night showed about 60 percent stronger reactions to upsetting pictures in the amygdala, a brain area that responds to threats." Olivia picked it up from there. "So when I blew up at your joke, my brain was treating it like an actual threat, because I'd barely slept. I wasn't angry at you. My amygdala was turned up too loud."

Celina thought about it, pushing wet hair off her forehead. "So I could say anything this morning and you'd have exploded." "Basically anything." "Then I forgive you, but you owe me the last s'more."

They walked back through the dark together, and Olivia practiced what she'd decided to modify about her routine: lights out before anyone could pitch a second dock night, four slow breaths whenever her chest tightened before a race, and sleep treated as a real component of training, not the boring part. At the fire circle, Lacey was saving them a bench, waving. Olivia took one long breath in through her nose, let it out slow, and sat down between her friends as the flames popped.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: VisiCalc, written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston and released for the Apple II in 1979, was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers.
story:
Alexa sat at the kitchen table with her mom's old laptop open and a crumpled list beside her: babysitting money, birthday money, the twenty dollars from raking Mr. Zhou's leaves, all written in pencil across three weeks. She wanted a chart to show her dad, who had promised that if she could prove she was saving steadily, he would add ten dollars for every month she kept it up. The problem was that every time she added a number, she had to add the whole column again by hand.

She typed the numbers into a column and stared at the empty cell below them. There had to be a rule the program could follow, some hidden instruction, so the total would grow on its own. She typed an equals sign, then guessed, and the cell spat back an error. She tried another guess. Another error.

"You look like you're plumbing the depths of that thing," her grandfather said from the doorway, holding his teacup. He sat down across from her and peered at the screen.

"I want it to add the column by itself," Alexa said. "And then make bars."

He laughed quietly. "You know, your grandmother and I, back in 1979, we saw the first spreadsheet program for personal computers. VisiCalc. It ran on the Apple II. Two fellows wrote it, Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston. Before that we did the sums on paper, every single row."

Alexa stopped typing. "A whole program just for columns?"

"A whole program. You'd change one number and the total would change too. Your grandmother narrated the grocery budget out loud while I typed it in, month after month."

Alexa looked at the screen differently then. If people had wanted this exact thing badly enough to invent it, the rule must be simple and it must be findable. She was not being impulsive, jumping to some wild shortcut; she decided to test one small idea. She clicked inside the empty cell, found a button shaped like the Greek letter sigma, and clicked it. The program highlighted her whole column, as if it had recognized the shape of what she wanted. She pressed Enter, and the total appeared, exactly matching her pencil arithmetic. Then she highlighted the column again, clicked the chart button, and a bar graph rose up on the screen, each week a solid gray tower.

"Look," she said, turning the laptop toward her grandfather. The tallest bar was the birthday week, and the shortest was the week she had spent eight dollars on a scarf. She had forgotten about the scarf until the bar made it plain, sitting there, stubborn and small. "I'm saving," she said slowly, "except when I'm not."

Her grandfather raised his teacup toward the shortest bar. "Then that one's your homework," he said.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In the Sally-Anne test, first used in 1985, children from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it was moved while she was away.
story:
The poster by the community centre gym door said DISCOVERY DAY: SHOW US WHAT YOU FOUND OUT, and Ryan had signed up before he even knew what his project would be. That was the problem. Zayd had a volcano, Eliam had a homemade rudder that steered a model boat across the pool, and Ryan had three days and nothing. He was sulking over the sign-up sheet when his little cousin, who was four, marched past the front desk hunting for the toy corner.

"Ryan, watch this," Zayd said, grinning. He crouched by the cousin and told her a story. "There's a girl named Sally. She puts her marble in the red basket, then she goes outside. While she's gone, her mom moves the marble to the green box. When Sally comes back, where will she look for her marble?" The cousin pointed firmly at the green box. "There, silly." Zayd laughed, but Ryan pulled him toward the water fountain.

"Wait. She was right there when the mom moved it. Try somebody who didn't see." Zayd squinted. "Like who?" Ryan looked around the gym. Mr. Kelly, who ran the centre, was setting up folding tables, and a handful of little kids from the after-school program were stacking blocks by the window. "Them," Ryan said. He copied the story onto a card, word for word, red basket, green box and all, and borrowed a marble from the lost-and-found jar.

For the next two days he tested every small kid at the centre, always asking exactly the same question. The ones who were three pointed at the green box, where the marble really was. But the four-year-olds, almost every single time, said Sally would look in the red basket, where she had left it. Even though they knew it had moved. Even though the right answer was obvious. "I don't get it," Eliam said, watching a small boy say "red basket" with total confidence. "They know where it is. They just told you."

"It's not about knowing where it is," Ryan said slowly, testing the idea out loud like a hypothetical rope bridge he wasn't sure would hold. "It's about knowing what Sally knows. Maybe the little ones can't tell Sally's mind apart from their own yet." He said it and immediately wanted to check it, so he ran the story one more time on his cousin, but this time Sally stayed in the room and watched the mom move the marble. "Red basket," his cousin said. Then he had Sally leave, and she switched to green box. It wasn't guessing. Something changed right around age four.

On Saturday he stood at his table with the marble, the two containers, and a hand-drawn chart of his results. When parents asked, he let their kids try it instead of explaining first, so they could see the split for themselves and distinguish the young answers from the older ones. A woman with a clipboard paused at his chart. "This is the Sally-Anne test," she said. "First used in 1985." Ryan grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. Zayd thumped him on the shoulder and pointed at the ribbon table. "Go get in line."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties.
story:
Noemie sat at the kitchen table with her laptop open, but she wasn't doing homework. She was reading the same paragraph for the third time. It was from a science site her teacher, Ms. Pritchard, had linked at the bottom of a class announcement, and it said that the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties.

She thought about Tuesday. On Tuesday, Nelson had been goofing around near her locker, mimicking her laugh, and she had grabbed his binder and thrown it down the hall before she'd even decided to. Ms. Pritchard had given her lunch detention, and Nelson hadn't spoken to her since. She had told herself she couldn't have helped it, that it just happened. Now she wasn't so sure that "just happened" was the whole story.

"So it's like the pilot light is on but the stove isn't finished being built," she said to the kitchen at large. Her mother looked up from chopping onions and asked what she was muttering about. Noemie read the sentence out loud, then added, "The prefrontal cortex. That's what it's called. It's still developing until my twenties."

"Meaning you're not doomed, maybe," her mother said, turning back to the onions. "Meaning you have to build some of the controls yourself while the hardware catches up."

Noemie hated when her mom made it sound invasive, like she'd peered straight into the guilty part of Noemie's head. But she also couldn't stop thinking about it. If the planning part of her brain was still under construction, then maybe there was a frontier between impulse and action, a small gap she could guard, even at fourteen. She decided to test it. The test would be simple: the next time something made her want to react instantly, she would count to five first. Five seconds. That was all.

The chance came faster than she expected. Her phone buzzed on the table. A message from Lexy, with a screenshot of a group chat Noemie wasn't in, and the words "are you seeing what Nelson is saying about you?" Noemie's thumb was already moving toward the reply box, her whole chest hot. She put the phone face down instead. One, two, three, four, five. Then she picked it up and typed, "What exactly did he say? Send me the whole thing, not the screenshot." She hit send and set the phone down again, watching it like a kettle about to boil.

It buzzed almost at once.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of children's bones, are weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress.
story:
Hazel loved Friday practice most of all, because Friday meant relay starts and relay starts meant diving until her goggles fogged up. She was lining up for her ninth sprint start of the hour when Phillip climbed out of the pool early, rubbing his shoulder with the sour face of someone who had just found a dead bug in his sandwich.

"You did like forty starts today," Hazel said, perching on the block beside him. "Coach didn't stop you?"

"Coach is watching Quinn's lane." Phillip rolled his shoulder and winced. "It's been sore since Tuesday. Weird, though. I didn't hit anything. I just did start after start after start."

Hazel slid into the water to keep her spot warm while she thought. A sore shoulder with no fall and no collision was like a counterfeit dollar: it looked like an injury, but underneath something else was going on. Her older brother pitched for the town baseball team, and she remembered him getting pulled mid-game, furious, muttering that he felt fine. She paddled to the ladder and hauled herself up beside Phillip. "Remember when the baseball coach enforced that pitch limit on my brother? Same thing. It wasn't his muscles. My mom said it was his growth plates."

"Growth plates?" Quinn said, drifting over with his kickboard like a manatee with opinions.

"Areas of growing cartilage near the ends of kids' bones," Hazel said. "They're weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress."

"So my shoulder isn't even mad at the right thing," Phillip said, staring at his own arm as if it had lied to him.

"Exactly." Hazel was already building the test in her head. "Here's the idea. Skip starts for one whole week, just swim and turn. If the soreness fades, then it's the repetition and not something actually broken." She held up a finger before he could argue. "And if it doesn't fade, we tell Coach everything."

The week felt endless, mostly because Phillip complained about it at every practice in the lane-line hierarchy of grievances, from the slowest swimmer up to Quinn, who complained the loudest. He did flip turns until his cheeks were pink and grumbled that walking into the water like a tourist was humiliating. Hazel kept tally on the whiteboard by the filing cabinet: Day 1, sore. Day 3, less sore. Day 5, Phillip forgot to rub it at all, which Hazel considered data.

Friday came around again. Phillip stood on the block, toes curled over the edge, and Hazel leaned forward on hers. "Remember, one start. Then regular swimming. Limits."

"One start," he agreed. "And if it works, we tell Mr. Suzuki to put a cap on starts for the whole team." He raised his arms, the whistle shrieked, and he sliced into the water so cleanly that even the lifeguard leaned over to watch. Hazel squinted down through the churn, waiting to see whether he surfaced smiling or holding that shoulder again.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: During the fight-or-flight response, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up.
story:
The clock on Mr. Kim's wall said 2:14, and Lincoln's heart was pounding so hard he could feel it in his ears. His breathing had gone quick and shallow, like he'd run the mile in gym class, except he was sitting in a chair in the guidance counsellor's office holding a hall pass he'd forgotten to put down.

"Your heart's racing," Mr. Kim observed. He didn't sound worried, which somehow made it worse. "That happens before presentations a lot."

Lincoln nodded. Tomorrow he had to give his English presentation in front of the whole class, and his body had apparently decided the presentation was today. He'd felt the same thing before the debate in November, when April had leaned over and whispered that he'd gone pale. Back then he'd assumed he was coming down with something. He'd sat out lunch and gone home early, and afterward April hadn't spoken to him for a week because he'd left her to cover their joint argument alone. He still wasn't sure that leaving had been the right call, or the selfish one.

Mr. Kim slid a sheet of paper across the desk. It had a rough, approximate sketch of a body on it, with two small shapes marked near the top of the kidneys. "Adrenal glands," he said simply, and tapped the shapes. "Look up what they do when the fight-or-flight response kicks in. Tell me tomorrow if it matches what you're feeling."

That night Lincoln read until his mom made him turn off his lamp. When something scares you, or even something you merely despise, like public speaking, the adrenal glands release adrenaline into the blood. Adrenaline makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up. He sat with that for a while. His body wasn't broken. It was doing exactly what it was built to do, treating the classroom like a place with an antagonist in it, some wild animal crouching behind the projector. There was no animal. There was only Ariyah in the second row, who had once laughed at a presenter so meanly that a kid transferred out of English. Lincoln wrote a line in his notebook: pounding heart equals adrenaline, not danger. It was a hypothesis, and tomorrow was the test.

At 2:14 the next day, English class, Mr. Kim's clock just a wall away, Lincoln stood up. His heart was already hammering, and his breath came fast, and this time he knew why, knew it was chemistry and not fear, or not only fear. He walked to the front, breathed out slowly the way the counsellor's worksheet suggested, and looked at Ariyah.

"So," Lincoln said. "Question one."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In East Asian dining etiquette, chopsticks should not be left standing upright in a bowl of rice, because it resembles incense offered to the dead.
story:
Joshua had exactly forty minutes before the neighborhood potluck started, and the dumplings his grandmother had helped him fold that morning were still sitting in the fridge at Mr. Katz's house, where the long tables were being set up. He raced down the block with the container balanced on his palms, the way a waiter carries a tray, because last year he had dropped a plate of cookies on the sidewalk and that consequence was still burned into his memory. Precious waved from the driveway, doling out napkins and forks.

"We're distributing the silverware," she said, handing him a bundle. "Andrea's mom brought chopsticks for the noodle bowl. You're on table three."

Joshua set out forks and spoons, then took the small cup of chopsticks to the far table, where Andrea was arranging platters of food in careful rows. The room filled fast. People shook hands, bumped shoulders, kissed cheeks, depending on which family they came from, and Joshua noticed that Mr. Katz greeted everyone with a firm handshake and both hands around the other person's, a gesture he had never seen before. Precious's aunt arrived with a bowl of fruit, because at her grandmother's house you never came to a meal empty-handed, and a man from the corner store brought flowers and immediately asked if he could help wash dishes.

Joshua heaped a bowl of rice from the big cooker, then picked up a pair of chopsticks to practice before anyone watched. He speared them upright into the rice so his hands would be free to carry his plate, and he was turning away when he caught the look on Andrea's face. She pulled the chopsticks out and laid them flat across the bowl, quick and quiet.

"Don't stand them up in the rice," she said, keeping her voice low. "In East Asian dining etiquette, chopsticks standing upright in a bowl of rice look like incense offered to the dead."

"Oh," Joshua said. His ears went hot. "Sorry. Thanks for telling me." He thought about the rule while he ate, watching to see whether it held. When Mr. Katz, who had never used chopsticks in his life, tried to rest his pair upright in the noodles, Andrea caught it again, and when a little kid did it with the rice, her mother slid the chopsticks down flat without a word. Same pattern, every time, at every bowl. So it wasn't about Andrea being picky. It was a rule that ran underneath the whole table like plumbing under a floor, invisible but real, and now that he could see it, he couldn't unsee it.

There were ten minutes left before the raffle, and Joshua still had a job to do. His grandmother's dumplings had gone fast, and the empty platter needed returning to the kitchen. He grabbed it, then paused by the cooler, filled a cup of water, and carried both over to Mr. Katz, who was mopping up noodle broth with a slice of bread and looking a little lost among so many new customs.

"Your first potluck on our street?" Joshua asked, holding out the cup.

Mr. Katz took it with both hands, the way he greeted people. "It's a fertile place for learning," he said, and Joshua laughed and sat down beside him with the empty platter on his knees.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The nucleus in an onion cell shows up as a small, round, darker spot, and it holds the cell's genetic material, DNA.
story:
Edouard crouched at the edge of the pond, holding the class microscope like it was a bowl of soup that might spill. Mr. Sutherland had marched them out here to the old settlement site on the far bank, where the school kept a patch of wild onions growing in the cracked foundations of vanished houses. "Collect, stain, observe, label," Mr. Sutherland had said, and then he sat down on a rock with his sandwich, leaving the rest to them.

Tye peeled a paper-thin layer of skin from an onion bulb and laid it on a slide. Dania dropped the iodine stain on and pressed the cover slip down with the edge of her pencil, exactly the way the sheet of instructions showed. Edouard carried the slide to the flat stone where the microscope stood, out of the wind, and started to focus. A cold draft came off the water and made his hands slow and careful.

At first there was nothing but grey blur. Then the knob caught, and the view snapped into rows of brick-shaped cells, neat as a wall. Edouard drew them in his notebook, and Tye leaned over his shoulder. "Wall around the outside," Tye said, tapping the page. "Then the thin line inside that, that's the membrane. Easy marks." But Dania was frowning at the eyepiece, and when she lifted her head she looked hesitant, like she was about to say something wrong.

"There's a dot in every cell," she said slowly. "A little dark spot. Is that dirt? Because if I label dirt as a cell part, Mr. Sutherland will laugh at me in red pen." Tye snorted. "Probably your fingerprint, or onion grime. Skip it." Edouard thought about that. Dirt would land in one place, maybe two, the way crumbs land on a table. He looked again. The dot sat in nearly every cell, small, round, darker than everything around it. Things that show up in every single cell, in the same spot, doing the same thing, are probably not accidents. "It's in all of them," he said. "Dirt doesn't do that. I think it's a real part."

Mr. Sutherland wandered over, chewing, and looked at Edouard's labelled drawing, where he had written NUCLEUS beside the dot and, underneath, in careful letters, holds the cell's DNA. "So what convinced you?" he asked. "The pattern," Edouard said. "It's everywhere, so it must be doing something." Mr. Sutherland raised an eyebrow at Dania's notebook, where she had crossed out the word dirt and written a correction. "I'll have you know," she said, "that my onion was very clean." Tye picked up another slide, and behind them a frog plopped into the pond, sending rings across the water toward the far bank.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food banks usually rotate stock by 'first in, first out', sending older items out before newer ones so less food expires on the shelves.
story:
The neighborhood cleanup ended at noon, and Mr. Esposito pointed the last few volunteers toward the church basement where the food bank shared space with the recycling bins. Brayden followed Matilda and Vivaan down the steps, still smelling of garbage bags and grass clippings. Matilda wanted the sorting table because her older sister worked there and she liked to seem like an expert. Vivaan just wanted wherever the snacks were.

"Shelf duty," Mr. Esposito said, handing Brayden a crate of canned beans stamped with this month's date. "Beans go with the beans."

Brayden found the bean shelf and did what seemed sensible. He slid the old cans to the back and stacked the fresh ones in front, where people could see the clean labels, and he was still admiring the straight rows when Matilda came over.

"You did it backwards."

"I did it neatly."

"Mr. Esposito makes everyone redo it. Watch."

She pulled a can from the back, one that had been sitting there for months, and pushed the whole new row behind it. "It's first in, first out," she said. "Older items go out before newer ones so less food expires on the shelves."

Brayden looked at his ruined rows. He wanted to argue, but then he thought about the back of his own pantry at home, where a jar of pickles from two years ago hid behind the new ones and nobody ever touched it. If people took from the front, whatever sat behind stayed. The shelf worked the same way, only here the front had to hold the oldest cans, not the newest, or the back ones would rot in the dark where nobody checked. It felt like a rule someone should have told him. Nobody had, so he tested it. He lifted the new beans out, counted the old ones, and rebuilt the row with the oldest cans in front, faces turned out so the dates were visible.

"Huh," Matilda said. "You're faster than Vivaan."

Vivaan appeared with an armful of coffee tins and no snacks. "These don't fit anywhere. The shelf's full."

Brayden checked the dates on the tins. One was from last spring, and its label showed a green hillside and the words "grown near the equator." The other two were this year's. He pulled the oldest tin forward, wedged the new ones behind it, and said, "Rotate it. Old in front."

"I was going to put the pretty ones first," Vivaan said.

"The date decides, not the label."

Mr. Esposito came down the aisle with his clipboard, stopped at the bean shelf, and ran a finger along the front row. He checked the dates, then checked the back, then looked at Brayden for a long second. "Coffee next," he said. "The crates are by the freezer. Don't let anyone restrict you to beans."

Brayden carried the clipboard list to the freezer corner, Matilda trailing behind, arguing about who got to handle the soup.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
story:
The sports bar smelled like buffalo sauce and onions, and Charlotte's little brother was already stuffing napkins into his water glass like a tiny carnivore who had never seen food before. Their father had claimed a booth beneath the biggest screen, where the announcers were going on about a guard whose three point shooting had "improved by 25 percent this season." Charlotte was only half listening. Her half of the bet with her brother was that she could figure out something before the wings arrived, and his half was his dessert for a week.

The something was on her phone. Two stories about the same poll had shown up in her feed that morning, one saying support for the new stadium had risen 10 points, the other saying it had risen 25 percent. Her brother had immediately declared both headlines counterfeit journalism, written by people who couldn't agree on anything. Their father had laughed and said one of them had to be wrong, and that was when Charlotte, who did not enjoy being told things had to be wrong when they didn't, made the bet.

"So which is it, ten or twenty five?" her brother asked, mouth already full of bread. "The stadium people can't even count."

Charlotte scrolled between the two stories. The poll numbers were right there in both. Last month, 40 percent of people supported the stadium. This month, 50 percent. Same poll, same people, two different headlines. She grabbed a napkin before her brother could sacrifice it to his water glass art.

"It's ten," she said slowly, reading. "Forty to fifty is ten points higher. Both stories say that." She turned the phone so he could see. He shrugged and kept chewing, which prolonged the whole process of getting anywhere with him.

"But twenty five is also right," she said. She looked up at the screen, where the guard's face floated beside his stats. "That's why they said his shooting improved 25 percent. Because that's the increase." She scribbled 40 and 50 on the napkin and circled both numbers, then pushed the napkin across the table like evidence.

Her brother squinted at it. "Ten and twenty five aren't the same number, Charlotte."

"They're the same change," she said. "Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points, and also a 25 percent increase. Both headlines are true. They're just talking differently."

Her father had gone quiet somewhere around the word percentage. He picked up the napkin, held it at arm's length, and read it over the top of his glasses like it might be a counterfeit fifty. "Huh," he said finally. "So the story I read this morning wasn't lying to me."

"It was just in a different mood," Charlotte said.

The wings arrived, and her brother, mouth full, gestured at the dessert menu with a sauce-stained finger in a way that clearly meant he was not surrendering anything yet. Charlotte slid the napkin into her jacket pocket anyway, next to her phone, and watched the guard sink a shot on the big screen while her father flagged the waiter and ordered a second basket.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: In a healthy onion cell, the cell membrane is pressed tightly against the inside of the cell wall, which makes the membrane very hard to see as a separate line.
story:
Marcus had been staring into the eyepiece for five minutes, and the deadline was ticking: the bus back to school left the trailhead in twenty minutes, and Ms. Lewandowski had already called the first warning. His lab sheet had three labels to finish, cell wall, nucleus, and cell membrane, and he had found the wall easily, a tidy rectangle around every cell. The nucleus showed up as a dense gray blob once he fine-tuned the focus. But the membrane was nowhere.

"Do onion cells even have one?" he muttered.

Denis leaned over from the next station, where the teacher had set up three field microscopes on a folding table beside the creek. "They have to. It's on the sheet." Denis wanted the full ten points, because his grade had started to deteriorate after he skipped two labs, and today was his chance to fix it. "Check the edges of your slide. Mine has junk floating around out there."

Carina, sketching the trail map for her own sheet, didn't look up. "Ten minutes, Marcus."

Marcus panned the stage slowly toward the edge of the coverslip, where the iodine stain ran thin. His search had been in vain so far, and he was beginning to think his whole slide was bad. Then a thought stopped him. Every cell he'd seen was a neat brick, perfect and plump. What if the membrane was there all along, pressed flat against the inside of the wall, so tight it just didn't show as its own line? A healthy cell would hide it. A damaged one might not.

He said it out loud, half to himself. "If it's pressed right against the wall, you wouldn't see it as a separate line. You'd need a cell that's coming apart."

Denis frowned. "So find a broken one. There were some mushy bits at the edge of the onion when we cut it."

Marcus rotated the fine focus and hunted along the ragged rim of the tissue. Most cells near the edge had started to deteriorate, their walls wrinkled, and a few had split. Then he found it: one cell with a small fracture in the wall, and inside, a thin line peeling inward, following the wall's shape but curling away from it, just barely its own border.

"There," Marcus said. He drew the cell quickly, labeling the wall, the drifting nucleus, and the line inside the break. "Cell membrane. It's pressed up against the wall in the healthy ones, so tight you can't see it separate."

Denis scrambled back to his own eyepiece, hunting his slide's edges, and gave a low whistle. Carina abandoned her map and crowded in to look, changing her mind about finishing the sketch first. "Draw it for me later?" she said.

"Bus in five," Ms. Lewandowski called from the trail.

Marcus capped the pen, slid the cover slip into the disposal jar, and carried his labeled sheet toward the folding table, one hand still cupped over the paper so the wind off the creek couldn't take it.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: The United States Senate never ratified the Treaty of Versailles, so the United States never joined the League of Nations, the peacekeeping body the treaty created.
story:
Tyler had his history textbook open on the kitchen table, a blank notecard beside it, and twenty minutes before his mom drove him to the study group. Mr. Levy was making the class present tomorrow, and the topic on the notecard was supposed to be how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War. Tyler read the paragraph twice and it still felt like soup, everything swirling together with no handle to grab.

He called Harman, who answered out of breath from lacrosse practice. "I don't get it," Tyler said. "The treaty ended World War One, right? So how does ending a war start another one?"

"Um," said Harman, which was how all his history answers began. "Blame Germany? That's in there somewhere. Gotta shower, we'll figure it out at your house."

When the doorbell rang, Marika was standing there too, holding a bag of pretzels and her own notecard, which already had writing on three sides. She sat down, flipped to the diagram in the textbook, and tapped it. "Okay, so here's the part that broke my brain yesterday. The League of Nations. The treaty created it to keep peace after the war, like an international referee."

"Impartial?" Tyler asked.

"Exactly. And get this: the United States never joined it."

Tyler stared at her. "Wait. President Wilson helped plan the whole thing, and his own country just said no thanks?"

"The Senate never ratified the treaty," Marika said, crunching a pretzel. "I couldn't believe it either."

Tyler leaned back, trying to picture it. He couldn't see a peacekeeping body, whatever that looked like, but he could test the idea with something he could see. He grabbed a saltshaker and put it in the middle of the table. "Okay, the League is the saltshaker. And the United States is..." He spun around, took the enormous flashlight from the junk drawer, and set it apart from the saltshaker. "The biggest, brightest thing in the room, and it's over there, not helping."

"So the referee shows up without the strongest player," Harman said, pointing a pretzel at the flashlight. "Then the referee can't actually stop anybody from shoving."
