"Then the treaty's punishment part just sits there, and everybody's mad with nobody watching," Tyler said. He tried to evade looking at the clock on the microwave, but it caught him anyway: ten minutes until his mom came downstairs.

They divided it up fast. Marika would cover what the treaty did, Harman would explain the League of Nations, and Tyler would do the flashlight part, the piece he'd figured out himself. He wrote his lines on the notecard, then realized Marika's hands were shaking a little, and slid the pretzel bag toward her.

"Eat," he said. "You're presenting first, you need fuel more than I do."

His mom appeared at the bottom of the stairs, keys in hand, and Tyler swept the flashlight and saltshaker into his backpack. "Props," he said.

"Bring back my flashlight," she said, "or you're grounded until the next world war."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: In the dark, the eyes slowly grow more sensitive as rod cells in the retina rebuild a light-sensitive pigment called rhodopsin, which takes half an hour or more.
story:
When the lights died at seven o'clock, Sydney's little living room turned into a cave, and her cousin Braydon, who had been reading on the couch, let out a yelp that would have frightened an actual bear. She found the emergency candles in the hall closet by touch, set three of them on the coffee table, and lit them with the stove lighter. The flames gave a small orange circle of safety, but beyond it the whole room was black. Braydon held his hand six inches from his face and reported, with real alarm, "Syd, I can barely see my own fingers."

"Give it time," Sydney said, but she didn't actually know if that was true, and it bugged her. She remembered a science unit where Mr. Becker had mentioned that eyes adjust to the dark slowly, on purpose, rebuilding something over half an hour or more. She couldn't remember the word for it, which was worse. She texted Maxwell, who was a walking dictionary with terrible taste in music, and when his answer came back she read it aloud: "It's called rhodopsin. It's a pigment in your rod cells, the ones in your retina. Your eyes make more of it in the dark."

"So you're saying I have to sit here being blind while my eyeballs do chemistry?" Braydon said.

"Basically. Want to test it?" Sydney grabbed the conventional deck of cards from the drawer, shuffled it, and made Braydon try to name the suits by candlelight. He got two out of ten and guessed "red" for a black card, which they both agreed was pathetic. She set a timer for thirty minutes, and to pass the time they invented a game where Braydon had to narrate her favourite show like a movie villain, complete with an evil antagonist voice. His impression of the villain was so bad that Sydney had to compress herself into a pillow to muffle her laughing, since the neighbours probably thought the house was empty and haunted.

When the timer buzzed, she blew out two of the three candles, carried the deck to the far side of the room where the light barely reached, and dealt ten cards face down on the bookshelf. Braydon shuffled over, squinted, and named the suits one by one. Eight out of ten. He could see the edge of the couch, the shape of the armchair, even the cat, who had been invisible all evening and was now glaring at both of them from the windowsill like a furry antagonist of her own.

"Half an hour," Braydon said, holding up the deck like a trophy. "My eyeballs finished their chemistry homework."

The lights snapped back on, blinding white, and both of them screamed. When Sydney's vision cleared, Braydon was standing there with ten cards scattered across the floor, and every single one of them, she realized as she bent to look, was a heart. "You switched the deck," she said. "You absolute cheater." He grinned, held up the queen of hearts he'd been palming all along, and said, "Takes half an hour to see in the dark. Takes two seconds to fool your cousin."

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: French political scientist Maurice Duverger observed that first-past-the-post elections tend to produce two large parties, an idea now called Duverger's law.
story:
Marcus had lost the mock election at the community centre three weeks in a row, and he was tired of it. His club, the Green Raptors, had gotten eleven votes out of forty. That was more than a quarter of the room, and it had earned them exactly zero seats on the youth council.

"Count again," he said, sliding the ballot box across the table to Hussain. They were in the craft room, where Ms. Suryanto had taped a big sheet of paper to the wall with all the results written in marker. Hussain counted the slips twice and shrugged.

"Eleven. The Blue team got eighteen and won both seats." Hussain winced as he said it, because he had voted Green himself.

Marcus stared at the sheet. Under first-past-the-post, which was how Ms. Suryanto had run the vote, the room was split into three districts, and whoever got the most votes in each district took the seat. The Blues had a majority in two districts. The Raptors had spread their voters thin, like butter scraped over too much bread. "What if we counted all the votes together?" he asked. "Forty votes, two seats. Twenty votes per seat."

Skye, who was sprawled on the floor drawing an intricate map of an imaginary island, sat up. "Then eleven votes should get you, like, half a seat. And the Reds have nine, so they'd get almost half too. Nobody would be shut out." She grabbed a marker and wrote the numbers under the old ones. "That's proportional whatever-it's-called. Proportional representation."

Ms. Suryanto passed through with a stack of books for the shelf and dropped one on the table without a word, the way she did when she wanted them to find something themselves. Marcus flipped it open. The index sent him to a page about a French political scientist named Maurice Duverger, who had observed that first-past-the-post elections tend to produce two large parties.

"It's called Duverger's law," Skye read over his shoulder.

Marcus felt the idea move through him like a slow shiver, the same feeling he got when a math problem suddenly made sense, the kind of understanding that travels straight to your intestine and stays there. Small parties didn't lose because their ideas were bad. They lost because of the counting rule itself, and Duverger had seen it happen over and over.

"So we've been playing on a tilted field," he said. "Every single time." He copied the vote numbers onto a fresh sheet, then drew two columns: one for the way they had voted, one for the proportional way. The Raptors got a seat in the second column. The Reds did too.

Ms. Suryanto was straightening the marker bin across the room. Marcus picked up the fresh sheet and walked toward her, holding it out in front of him like evidence.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Aaron opened his laptop, went straight to his account, and clicked the padlock icon again, as if it might have changed overnight. It still said private. So how had his photo of last Saturday's skate session ended up on a page he had never heard of, with his neighborhood in the caption?

He remembered accepting a follower named Dex two weeks ago. Flashback: he'd been at the kitchen table, tapping approve on a dozen requests because it felt good to watch the number climb. He'd never messaged Dex once.

He pulled up his messages and typed to Miller: "did u forward my skate pic anywhere?"

"No. Why?"

Aaron sent the link. Three dots appeared, then vanished, then appeared again.

"that's not me," Miller wrote. "check Karlee."

Karlee answered in a minute. "I only sent it to Dex bc he asked if that was our spot. I thought he went to Ridge."

Aaron sat back. His account was private, so only followers could see the post. But Karlee was a follower, and she had shared it to someone outside without even thinking. Being private hadn't stopped anything once the picture was already in someone else's hands. He tested it: he posted a blank gray square, waited an hour, and asked Miller to forward it to his own second account. It arrived there instantly, no lock, no warning, no note saying where it came from.

He opened the page that had reposted his skate photo and scrolled. Whoever ran it seemed to monitor spots around town, tagging locations like a parallel list of where kids hung out. The skate park. The gas station with the slushie machine. The creek path. His stomach went tight and small.

He called Karlee, because typing was too slow. "You have to stop sending my stuff to people you don't actually know."

"I didn't know it mattered. Your account's private."

"That only limits who sees my posts. Anyone I already let in as a follower can still copy or share whatever they see." He heard her breath catch. "Please just delete it from the chat."

"There," she said. "Deleted."

He removed Dex as a follower, then went through the whole list, tapping remove on every name he couldn't match to a face. Nineteen approvals became six. Then he stripped the location tag off every photo still on his page, starting with the skate park.

Ms. Farah from next door knocked on the doorframe of the kitchen, holding a printed flyer about the school's proposed phone policy amendment, whatever that was, and asking if his mom was home. Aaron looked past her at the screen, at the gray square post still sitting there untouched, and closed the laptop lid.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: The placebo effect is when people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, simply because they expect it to help.
story:
Cale slapped a shiny blue can onto the lab table before the bell even rang. "Two-tenths of a second," he said. "That's how much faster I ran yesterday, right after I drank this. Isa, you're slow, you should try it."

Xavier picked up the can and turned it over. The label promised SPEED, FOCUS, POWER in letters the size of his thumb, but the ingredient list was mostly caffeine, sugar, and things he couldn't pronounce. Isa leaned over to look too. "My brother says that stuff is just expensive soda," she said.

"Then explain my time," Cale said. Xavier couldn't, exactly, but something about it bothered him. Cale had also been telling everyone all week that the drink was going to make him faster. He had practically been bragging about the race before he ran it. Xavier flipped open his notebook and wrote two questions at the top of a fresh page. Did the can make Cale faster, or did believing in the can do it? Then he raised his hand.

Ms. Rahman stopped by their table and listened while Xavier explained, feeling his ears go warm halfway through. "If you want to test that," she said, "you'll need a design that isn't just one person's story. Think about what would make your evidence robust enough to convince someone else." She glanced at the clock. "And you'll need runners."

Recruiting volunteers turned out to be the easy part. At lunch, Xavier signed up six kids from the track team, including Cale and Isa, and promised them each a "performance drink" before their time trials on Thursday. What he didn't tell them was that every cup would contain plain orange juice. If the drink was what mattered, nobody should get faster. If believing was what mattered, that was a different answer entirely.

Thursday after school, the runners drank, waited ten minutes, and sprinted the hundred meters while Xavier clicked the stopwatch and Isa called out times. Cale beat his old mark again, and so did two others. Xavier stared at his clipboard. Three of six improved, all three of them kids who had been talking all day about how the drink would help. The other three ran almost exactly their usual times.

"See!" Cale said, chest still heaving. "It works."

"It was juice," Xavier said quietly. "There was nothing in it but juice." He let that sit while Cale's face went from triumphant to confused to something more thoughtful. "It's called the placebo effect," Isa said, reading off Xavier's notebook, where he'd written it in careful letters that morning. "People feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, like a sugar pill, just because they expect it to help." Cale looked at the empty cup in his hand, then at the track.

"So next time," he said slowly, "maybe I just believe in orange juice."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Details in the background of a photo, such as a street sign, a house number or a school logo, can let a stranger work out where it was taken.
story:
Gabriel had one job at the mall: find the limited-edition sneakers, take one photo, and get first in line to post it to the ShoeRadar contest before anyone else. Uriah and Cian had come along as lookouts, mostly because Cian wanted a pretzel.

"They're in the window," Uriah said, pointing at the sports store. "You have to be in the photo too, right? Contest rules."

"Photo has to include you and the shoes," Gabriel said. "That's it." He lined himself up beside the display, phone out, grinning like a man who had just won something. Then Cian coughed.

"Dude. Your mom works at the mall information desk. Everyone knows that desk. It's in the background."

Gabriel lowered the phone. The photo had caught the storefront, the display, his own face, and behind him, the big blue information kiosk with the mall map and the desk where his mom sat every weekday, wearing a name tag with her full name on it.

"So?" he said.

"So, so," Cian said, waving his pretzel. "You're going to post that online. Strangers look at that stuff. They zoom in. There's the map, there's your mom's name, and boom, anyone can figure out exactly where you are, and that you know somebody who works here."

Gabriel didn't believe it at first. He inhale-d the last of his soda just to have something to do with his hands. Then, standing by the fountain, he opened the photo again and pinched the screen to zoom in. The mall map was blurry but readable: STORE YOU ARE HERE, the little red star, the name of the shopping center printed across the top. Behind his mom's desk, on the wall, hung a poster that said CONGRATULATIONS TO OUR EMPLOYEE OF THE MONTH, and though her face was small, her name tag was not. He could read every letter.

"Huh," he said.

"Also," Uriah said, "there's a mirror in the display. You can see the entrance sign reflected in it. The one with the street name."

Gabriel tested it, because testing was faster than arguing. He took a new selfie in front of the fountain instead, with nothing behind him but water and pennies, and showed it to Uriah. "Better?"

"Where's the shoes?"

"Out of frame. Contest broken." Gabriel tried again, angling so the sneaker display showed beside him but the storefront sign, the mall map, and his mother's entire workplace stayed out of the shot. It took four tries. Cian ate his pretzel with the patience of a monk.

On the fourth try Gabriel got it: him, the sneakers, a stretch of plain wall. He checked every corner of the frame, zooming until the pixels turned mushy, and found nothing but beige. He posted it, then sat down on the fountain's edge, where the three of them watched the likes climb in the contest feed.

At first the comments were the usual hierarchy, the fast posters on top and the slow ones buried. Then a new comment appeared from an account with no picture: "Nice shoes, Gabriel. Say hi to your mom at the info desk for me."

Gabriel's stomach dropped. His account name was just his first name, and the photo had no desk in it. He scrolled back through his older posts, the dormant ones from weeks ago, until he found it: a selfie he'd taken at home before leaving, standing on the front porch, proud of his outfit. In the background, clear as day, hung the house number, and the street sign stood at the corner behind his shoulder.

He deleted it. Then he deleted three more, one by one, working fast, while Cian leaned over his shoulder.

"So," Cian said, "pretzel's gone. What now?"

"Now," Gabriel said, "we go home the long way. And I take photos of walls."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A thesis should be narrow enough to prove in the space available; a claim about all sports everywhere is too broad for a short essay.
story:
Parker sat at the corner table of the public library with his essay prompt in front of him: two pages on whether technology helps or hurts kids. He had written one sentence so far, "Technology affects everything," and had been staring at it for twenty minutes. Across from him, Ciara was supposed to be working on her own paper, but she kept sliding her pencil back and forth like a tiny diplomat negotiating between boredom and homework.

"I think it's a solid thesis," Parker said.

"It's the size of a planet," Ciara said. "You can't prove a sentence like that in two pages. You'd need a hundred pages, and you'd still be wrong somewhere."

Marion dropped into the third chair with a stack of books about soccer. "Ms. Qureshi rejected my thesis yesterday," she said. "I wrote that sports are good for everyone in the whole world. She said a claim about all sports everywhere is too broad for a short essay. She made me narrow it down to one thing I could actually prove."

Parker looked at his sentence again. Technology, everything. He tested a smaller idea: "Technology helps kids my age with homework." Still big. He cut it further: "Text reminders from teachers raise homework turn-in rates at our school." That felt like something he could actually support with a source, not something he'd have to incorporate half the internet to defend.

The twist arrived as Ms. Qureshi passed their table and glanced at Marion's new thesis, which read: "Soccer is the best sport that has ever existed, in all countries, forever."

"Marion," she said mildly, "we discussed this."

"I was testing whether you were paying attention," Marion said, and her grin was so infectious that even Ms. Qureshi laughed before walking on.

Parker changed his mind about his own cleverness somewhere in the next hour. His first outline had three points, but the third point, "technology is the future," turned out to be another planet-sized claim hiding in his list. He crossed it out and replaced it with survey data from the front office about homework turn-in. When Ciara leaned over to check, she nodded slowly, which from Ciara was a standing ovation.

At closing time, Parker copied his narrowed thesis onto a clean index card and slid it into his binder. "Two pages," he said, holding up two fingers like a promise. "I can prove this in two pages."

Marion held up one finger. "I can prove mine in one. Soccer is the best sport, at this table, right now." She pointed at Parker's terrible gym performance from Tuesday, and he threw a foam dart from the library's prize box at her head.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A control group gets no change at all, giving a baseline to compare the tested groups against.
story:
Riley knelt in the backyard with six bean plants lined up on an old plank, each one in a labeled cup. Two got the fancy fertilizer Tye had donated, two got half-strength fertilizer, and two got nothing but water and sunshine. He had almost skipped those last two. They felt like a waste of space, plants doing nothing while the others did the experiment.

"Those ones look sad," Amine said from the porch steps, where he was supposed to be measuring but was mostly eating crackers.

"They're supposed to look sad," Riley said. "That's the point." He wasn't entirely sure he believed himself. Last year, for the fifth-grade fair, he had grown three plants with different amounts of light and won nothing, because the judge kept asking how he knew the tall one was tall because of the light instead of the soil or the seed. He hadn't had an answer then. He had been thinking about that question all week.

Mr. Sokolov, the neighbour whose fence backed onto the yard, leaned over the rail. "Six cups," he said. "You have a favorite?"

"The fertilized ones," Riley admitted. "I want them to win."

Mr. Sokolov smiled but said nothing more, which was annoying, because his silence had a way of enforcing honesty. Riley looked at the two plain-water cups again. Those were the ones the judge would ask about, if the judge was anything like last year's. Two plants that got no change at all, sitting there like a baseline, so you could compare the tested ones against them. His instinct said to shove them behind the plank where nobody would look. He left them in front instead.

Then Tye arrived with a grocery bag and an idea. "What if we spray all of them with the plant food too? Then maybe they all grow huge and we definitely place."

Riley shook his head slowly. "If we change all six, we lose the comparison. The plain-water ones are called the control group." He tapped the two untouched cups. "No change at all for these. That's how we'll know the fertilizer actually did something."

Tye frowned at the bag in his hands. "So my extra spray was pointless."

"Keep it for the volatile stuff," Riley said, nodding at the half-strength cups, where one seedling had sprouted crooked and one had sprouted fine. Already the fertilized group wasn't behaving: one tall and glossy, one yellowing at the edges. Without the control cups, he'd have no way to see that something besides fertilizer was going on.

Amine finally stood, brushing cracker crumbs off his jeans, and crouched beside the plain-water pair. "So we just watch these do nothing?"

"We watch them do nothing really carefully," Riley said, and pulled out the notebook where he'd ruled a chart with six columns. He wrote the date at the top, then knelt down with the ruler and measured the first control plant, pressing the flat end gently into the soil. "Four centimeters," he said aloud. "Write it down before I forget."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A baking soda volcano erupts because baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) reacts with vinegar (acetic acid) to produce carbon dioxide gas.
story:
Paige spread the newspaper across the kitchen table and set down the clay mountain she had spent two evenings shaping. Zorawar had appointed her volcano engineer for the science fair, mostly because her kitchen had the biggest table, but also because he trusted her to make things work.

"This is fine," Zorawar said, poking the crater, "but everyone brings a volcano. It fizzes, it oozes, judges nod, done. I want ours to do something nobody else's does."

"Like what?" Paige asked.

"Like, what if we made it erupt harder or softer on purpose? Not just dump stuff in and hope." He pulled out a notebook and drew three columns. "We measure."

They started with what Zorawar already knew from his older sister's chemistry book. "Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate," he said, reading off his notes, "and vinegar is acetic acid. When they mix, they make carbon dioxide gas. That's the eruption."

"So the gas is what pushes the foam out," Paige said slowly, watching the little red pool in the crater. She couldn't see the gas itself, only what it did, the bubbles climbing over the rim like the fizz on soda. That gave her an idea. "If the gas pushes the foam, then more gas should mean a bigger eruption. And more gas should come from more vinegar. We can test that."

Zorawar made the plan explicit: one tablespoon of vinegar for the first trial, three for the second, five for the third, with the same amount of baking soda every time. They would record the height of each eruption against the pencil marks he had drawn on a ruler taped to the wall behind the volcano. Outside, on the back step, in case of mess.

The first eruption barely reached the crater's edge. The second one rose past the second pencil mark and splattered the newspaper. The third sent red foam nearly to the top of the ruler, and they both scrambled back, laughing, while it dribbled down the clay slopes.

"It went higher every single time," Zorawar said, writing fast.

"And the only thing we changed was the vinegar," Paige said. "Same soda, same volcano, same everything else." She looked at the three numbers in his notebook, one under another, climbing. That was the part she liked best, the pattern you couldn't see directly but could catch with a ruler and a notebook.

Her mother came out with dish towels and shook her head at the puddles, though she was smiling. "The weather app says precipitation tonight," she said. "You two are doing your own kind of storm out here."

At school on Monday, Mr. Rajapakse walked past their table twice during setup, and the second time he stopped. "Measure twice, then run it again," he suggested. "Judges like a result you can repeat."

So when the judge stopped at their booth, Zorawar held up the ruler and Paige poured the vinegar, and the volcano roared exactly as high as before.

"Five tablespoons," she said. "Same as last time."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12 and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers aged 13 to 18.
story:
The waiting room of the dental office had a sparse selection of magazines, one poster about fluoride, and a flyer encouraging families to get their flu vaccine before winter. Lea sat between her mom and Kallie, pressing her tongue against the ache in her jaw. For two weeks her teeth had hurt in the morning, and she had decided not to tell anyone, because telling meant questions.

"Lea Flores?" the assistant called. In the chair, under the bright light, Ms. Sánchez the hygienist leaned in and made a small surprised sound. "Your back teeth are worn, honey. Are you grinding at night?" Lea admitted she woke up with a sore jaw and a headache most days. Ms. Sánchez looked at her chart instead of her mouth for a change. "Grinding is often a sign of stress. I can't prescribe anything, but the dentist may suggest a mouth guard, and you might look at what's going on in your days." She paused. "And your nights. How much sleep do you get?"

Lea did the math right there in the chair, staring at the ceiling light. She went to bed at eleven and got up at six thirty for school. Seven and a half hours. She had read in health class that kids aged six to twelve need nine to twelve hours, but she was thirteen now, a teenager, and teenagers needed eight to ten. Seven and a half was short even of that. So it wasn't only the volleyball tryouts, or the geometry test she kept worrying about at midnight. A hidden cause, and she had missed it because she'd been using the wrong number.

She tested the idea. That week she moved her phone charger to the kitchen, set a nine o'clock alarm that meant lights out by ten, and when she felt her shoulders climb toward her ears before a test, she breathed in for four counts and out for six, like the counselor's poster said. On Friday, Ms. Sánchez spotted her at the grocery store and asked about her jaw. "Better," Lea said, and it was true. The mouth guard helped too, though it made her look like a hockey player, and Kallie laughed so hard at the sleepover that she spilled her popcorn.

The cost was real, though. The group chat went on without her after ten, and by Monday Kallie was quoting jokes Lea had missed, our jokes, she thought, gone without her. But her head didn't ache, and at tryouts she caught the ball that used to sail past her. That night she plugged her phone into the kitchen outlet, and from the hallway she could hear her dad say, "Who's still texting at midnight?" Kallie's name lit up on the screen.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one.
story:
Liam stared at his phone in the kitchen, rereading the message he'd sent Daven twenty minutes ago: "Okay. See you tomorrow." Daven's reply had been cold. "Fine." Then nothing. Liam's little brother banged his spoon against his cereal bowl until their mom told him to knock it off, and Liam slipped the phone into his pocket and walked to Daven's house, three streets over, to figure out what he'd done wrong.

Daven opened the door but stood in the doorway like a guard hired to supervise the entry of strangers. "What," he said.

"What's wrong with you?" Liam asked. "I just said okay."

"You said Okay. With a period. Like a judge."

Liam pulled out his phone and showed him the screen. "It's the same word. Okay, okay. It's punctuation."

Daven crossed his arms. "It doesn't read the same. My aunt texts 'No.' when she's furious. My mom texts 'no' and it's fine. Period means mad. Everybody knows that."

"Everybody does not know that," Liam said, though an acute unease was creeping over him, because he had felt the same thing himself and never once said it out loud. He thought of all the flat, closed little messages that had ended in dots. Was there a pattern here, or were they both inventing a rule out of one bad afternoon?

They took it to Elena, who was spread across her driveway with a science fair poster and a marker that had stained three of her fingers blue. She listened, then held out her hand for the phone. "Try it," she said. "Send me 'okay' no period. Then send me 'Okay.' with one. Same word, both times."

Liam sent both. Elena read them in silence, then frowned. "The first one sounds like a friend. The second one sounds like you're canceling my birthday."

"See!" Daven shouted.

"But feelings aren't proof," Elena said, and dug through the shoebox of articles she'd printed for her poster. She flipped past a page about birds, then held one up. "Here. A small study from 2016. Binghamton University researchers found that the same text message ending with a period was seen as less sincere than the message without one. So it's not just Daven being dramatic."

Daven looked wounded. "I'm never dramatic."

Liam copied the sentence into his notes, then typed a new message to Daven while standing right in front of him: "sorry about the period. that was my formal voice. this is my porch voice." Daven watched the words appear, and his shoulders came down from around his ears. He typed back, "acceptable. no period detected." Elena capped her marker and said, "Now help me with this poster, both of you, before I tell the anecdote of the time Liam signed a group chat message 'Sincerely.'"

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In Spanish, "para llevar" means "to take away," so a customer who wants food to go asks for it "para llevar."
story:
Emily had forty minutes, because after school she had to pick up her mom's prescription at the pharmacy before it closed, and Friday she had to order lunch, out loud, in Spanish, at a real restaurant with Ms. Bouchard's whole Spanish class watching. That left tonight in the school library, a laminated menu from Casa Verde, and two friends who had agreed to help by being extremely unhelpful.

"You're overreacting," said Marilyn, sliding a plastic tray across the table like a waitress. "It's just lunch."

"You're immune to embarrassment," Emily said. "Some of us are not."

Fatimah sat on the other side of the table with the menu and a shoebox of props, which included a ketchup packet, a paper napkin, and two actual dinner plates she had taken from the cafeteria without anyone asking questions. "Okay, I'm the waiter. Buena tarde. Order."

Emily looked at the menu. "Quiero un taco. Y, um, un agua." She dug in her pocket for the play money they had made in class, coins drawn on scrap paper. "Cuánto cuesta?"

"Cuesta ocho dólares." Fatimah placed the taco, a folded napkin standing in for one, onto a real dinner plate and pushed it across the table with ceremony.

Emily stared at it. "I'm not eating here. We eat on the bus after the restaurant. Remember? Ms. Bouchard said we only get forty minutes and then we board the bus back, so the food comes with us."

"So take the plate."

"I can't take a plate on a bus."

Marilyn leaned back in her chair, balancing a pencil on her chin. "So say that."

Emily tried. "Um, no plate, bus, uh, comida, bus?" Fatimah, playing it straight, set a fork next to the plate. This was going to be a long forty minutes.

She postponed the panic and went at it like a science problem instead. There had to be a pattern, a fixed thing people said, because millions of people got food to go every day and they did not describe buses. She pulled the Spanish phrase book off the shelf beside Ms. Bouchard's desk and flipped to the food section. Halfway down the page, next to a small drawing of a paper bag, she found it. "Here. Para llevar. It says para llevar means to take away. That's the whole thing. Two words."

"Try it," said Fatimah, gathering up the plates.

"Quiero un taco y un agua, para llevar."

Fatimah swept the plates away and handed her the napkin folded inside the ketchup packet, which was apparently a bag now. "Su orden, para llevar."

"Cuánto cuesta?"

"Ocho dólares."

Emily counted out eight paper coins. Then she did the whole thing again, and then a third time with a different order, because once was luck and three times was knowing. Marilyn ordered a burrito para llevar just for the pleasure of saying it. Somewhere behind the desk, Ms. Bouchard looked up from her stamping, said nothing, and went back to it.

At the restaurant on Friday, Emily ordered her taco, paid for it, and heard herself add the last part without even thinking. The waiter put a paper bag on the counter. On the bus, she opened it and found they had given her two tacos. "Extra one," said Fatimah, reaching over. "Para llevar."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: A split is the time for one section of a race; an 800-metre runner's 400-metre split shows right away whether the first lap was faster or slower than planned.
story:
The running track circled the hockey rink like a shelf above the ice, six laps to every kilometre, and Scarlett had decided that tonight she would finally crack the eight hundred metres. Her problem was simple and stubborn: every time she raced it, she died on the second lap, legs full of sand, watching Ember pull away in the last hundred. She wanted, more than almost anything, to finish strong at the meet on Saturday.

"Stopwatch ready?" she asked Ember, who was leaning on the rail with Clarke's phone in one hand and Clarke beside her eating pretzels.

"Ready," Ember said. "Remember, your first split is your four-hundred time. That's the time for one section of the race, the first half. It shows right away whether your first lap was faster or slower than planned."

Scarlett nodded and toed the line at the Zamboni door. She remembered the summer, when she had timed herself around the duck pond and felt so good on lap one that she sprinted the whole thing, then stood bent over in the grass afterward, dizzy and furious. That was the pattern she could not see from inside her own body: the first lap felt easy exactly when it was ruinous. The second lap was where the bill came due.

She ran. The boards flashed past, cold air sliding off the ice and up over her ankles, and she concentrated on staying smooth. At the line Ember shouted, "Sixty-eight!" Scarlett nearly stopped. Sixty-eight seconds. Her plan had been seventy-five. She had gone out far too fast, and even though she felt fine, she knew from the number that the second lap would be a disaster. It was, sort of; she gritted her way home and finished collapsed against the boards while a mite hockey practice clattered on below.

"Sixty-eight," she panted. "But it felt slow. That's the trick of it."

"Your legs lie to you," Clarke said, offering a pretzel. "Nerves too. Before a race I get that hormone rush, adrenaline, and it makes everything feel light for about ninety seconds. Then it stops being generous."

"So the split is the only thing that tells the truth," Scarlett said. She sat down on the cold concrete and modified her plan on the back of her glove: not "run easy," which meant nothing, but "hit seventy-five," which meant everything. A too-fast first lap, she now understood, was corrosive; it quietly ate the second lap from the inside, and you never felt it until it was too late.

The twist came at Saturday's meet. She hit the line at seventy-five exactly, tucked in third, patient as winter, and with two hundred to go she was the only one who still had legs. She passed Ember, who was shouting something about splits, and then a girl in green from another school, and crossed the line with her chest out and the clock reading 2:29. Ember grabbed her at the fence, laughing, and said, "Negative split, almost. You ran the second half faster than the first." Scarlett looked back at the clock and asked, "Same track Tuesday?"

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic in 1973: people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
story:
Alexandre sat in the waiting room of the doctor's office with his sleeve already rolled up, because he was third in line for his flu shot. Everley, who was there for a checkup, slid into the chair beside him and lowered her voice. "My cousin got a shot last month and fainted in the parking lot. Smacked his head on the curb. He had to get staples." Alexandre winced. For the rest of the wait, every time the nurse called a name, the image of his cousin's head hitting the curb, an event he had never even witnessed, played behind his eyes like a film he couldn't switch off.

When his name was called, he asked the nurse to hold on a minute. She waited, arms crossed, while he pulled out his phone. "Quick question," he said. "How often do people actually faint after shots?" The nurse shrugged. "In fifteen years, I've seen it maybe four times, and two of those were teenagers who skipped breakfast." Behind her, a poster about immunization hung in a transparent plastic sleeve, and Alexandre stared at it while he typed: why do scary stories feel true.

The search gave him names. He read the page twice. "Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman," he said out loud. "Psychologists. Nineteen seventy-three. It's called the availability heuristic." Everley leaned over his shoulder. "What's that mean?" He scrolled, then turned the screen toward her. "People judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind." He counted on his fingers. "So your cousin's story pops up instantly because it's vivid. Meanwhile the thousands of uneventful shots, including every one I've ever had, leave no story at all. Nothing to remember."

Everley frowned. "But he did faint." "He did," Alexandre agreed. "But one example isn't evidence of a pattern." He decided to test it right there. Over the next ten minutes he asked three people in the waiting room whether they or anyone they knew had fainted after a shot. A man with a cast on his wrist said no. An older woman said her arm was sore once. Everley, asked last, had to admit her own shot history was boring. Three out of three, zero fainting, and the nurse's four in fifteen years on top of that.

The plague of the curb image had not vanished, but it had lost its grip, the way a shadow shrinks when you turn on a lamp. Alexandre rolled his sleeve higher and followed the nurse through the door. The needle went in, quick as a paper cut. He sat still, waited the suggested minute, and felt nothing happen at all. Then he walked back out and held up his bandaged arm toward Everley. "One more boring shot," he said. "Let's see you remember that in a month."

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: A motion is a formal proposal for a group to do something; under Robert's Rules, most motions need another member to second them before discussion begins.
story:
Alicia pushed her noodles around her plate and told her family about the science club disaster. "Last meeting, Marcus talked about the generator idea for twenty minutes," she said. "Nobody even wanted it, but we couldn't get off the topic. Mara never got to say anything about the greenhouse plan."

Her father paused with his fork in the air. "Twenty minutes? For one kid's idea?"

"That's the thing," Alicia said. "He just started talking, and everyone started arguing, and then it was time to go." She took a bite and chewed slowly, thinking. "Marcus didn't even have support. Nobody said they liked it first. So why did we discuss it at all?"

Her little brother was drawing a hurricane on his placemat, which gave Alicia an idea. At the next meeting, she handed out a page she'd made the night before. At the top it said Agenda, and under that, three numbered items. Julia read it upside down from across the table. "What's this?"

"A plan," Alicia said. "We go in order. And there's a rule." She'd found it in a dusty library book called Robert's Rules of Order, which smelled like her grandmother's attic. "If you want the club to do something, you make a motion. That's just a formal proposal," she said. "But before we discuss it, someone else has to second it. If nobody seconds it, we skip it."

Marcus, whose generator idea had consumed the last meeting, looked wounded. "So I need permission to talk?"

"You need one friend," Alicia said.

When Marcus stood up and proposed the generator again, the room went quiet in the humid, fanless way it did before a storm. Alicia counted to five in her head. Mara raised her hand.

"Second," Mara said, "but only so we can vote on it and move on. I want to get to the greenhouse."

They voted. The generator lost, three to eight, in about ninety seconds. Marcus sat down, and Julia leaned over and whispered, "That took less time than he spent describing the fan belt."

Mara's greenhouse plan came up next, and because everyone had already heard why the generator failed, the vote was quick and unanimous: the club would spend its ten dollars on seeds. Julia was named seed purchaser, since she lived near the garden store. She accepted the honor with a solemn nod, then asked if the ten dollars could maybe stretch to a snack on the way.

At dinner that night, Alicia reported the whole thing. Her father listened, nodded, and said, "So Marcus's idea got a fair vote."

"It did," Alicia said. "It just couldn't survive one." She speared her last noodle. "Mara says next month Julia's proposing a field trip with a stop at the ice cream place, and she already has three seconds lined up."
